claims.text: A thread is one path of execution inside a process; a process has at least one thread and can ask the operating system for more.
claims.source_hint: .NET fundamentals, Managed threading basics: what a thread is and the relationship between a process and its threads

claims.text: Threads of one process share that process's memory, so two of them can read and write the same variable or object without anything being copied between them.
claims.source_hint: .NET fundamentals, Managed threading basics / Managed threading best practices: threads of a process share the process's memory

claims.text: Task.Run queues the supplied code to the thread pool — worker threads the runtime keeps ready — and returns a Task that represents that work, while the calling thread carries on without running it.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Threading.Tasks.Task.Run(Action): queues the specified work to run on the thread pool and returns a Task; .NET fundamentals, Managed threading basics, The thread pool

claims.text: A local variable used inside a lambda is captured rather than copied, so both loops act on one counter; a local only the method uses can stay in its call frame, one still used by code outside that flow cannot, and the compiler places it on the heap instead.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference, Lambda expressions — captured variables; C# compiler messages, lambda expression errors (captured variables move to a heap-allocated closure object)

claims.text: Adding one to a variable is a read, an add and a write, not one indivisible step, so two threads can read the same value before either writes and one increment is then lost.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Threading.Interlocked, Remarks: Increment exists because a plain increment is not an atomic operation

claims.text: Because an increment can be lost this way but never invented, the total the sample prints after two loops of 100000 is at most 200000, is usually below it, and need not be the same on two runs.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Threading.Interlocked, Remarks; examples/don-hang at stage-0, samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Computer/ThreadsVsAsync.cs lines 11-15 (run it repeatedly)

claims.text: await Task.WhenAll(first, second) continues only once both supplied tasks have completed, and hands the thread back until then, as any await does.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Threading.Tasks.Task.WhenAll(Task[]): a task that completes when all of the supplied tasks have completed

claims.text: await hands the thread back for the length of the wait and records that the rest of the method should continue when the awaited operation finishes.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference, await operator; .NET asynchronous programming, Async in depth: what await does with the calling thread

claims.text: async and await do not create a thread; the two awaits in this sample ask for none — the Task.Run calls in the same method are what take pool threads.
claims.source_hint: .NET asynchronous programming, Asynchronous programming with async and await: the async keyword does not cause additional threads to be created

claims.text: Task.Delay(50) creates a task that completes after about 50 milliseconds, and awaiting it does not block the thread that reaches the await.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Threading.Tasks.Task.Delay(Int32), Remarks (the delay depends on the system clock); C# language reference, await operator

claims.text: After an await in a console program, the rest of the method may continue on a thread different from the one it ran on before the wait.
claims.source_hint: .NET asynchronous programming, Async in depth; .NET API reference, System.Threading.SynchronizationContext (a console app has none, so continuations run on a pool thread)

claims.text: Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId gets a unique identifier for the current managed thread.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference, System.Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId, Property value

claims.text: At stage-0 this sample is started with `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- threads-vs-async`, and the quoted lines are the signature and body of its RunAsync method.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs, the samples dictionary key threads-vs-async and the usage line above it

claims.text: At stage-0 the words "two threads added 200000" are fixed text in the sample's last WriteLine, so that sentence is printed whatever value the counter holds.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Computer/ThreadsVsAsync.cs line 15

claims.text: Two awaits written one after the other wait one after the other, so the time taken is about the sum of the two waits rather than the longer of them.
claims.source_hint: .NET asynchronous programming, Asynchronous programming with async and await: starting tasks before awaiting them versus awaiting each in turn

claims.text: In programs with a screen, one that stops responding is often a thread held inside a wait it could have handed back.
claims.source_hint: Stated as an opinion with its condition (programs with a screen); no source in content/versions.yaml quantifies how often this cause is behind such a symptom

claims.text: On a machine that can run two threads at the same moment, two loops handed to the thread pool by two Task.Run calls usually do overlap in time.
claims.source_hint: .NET fundamentals, Managed threading basics, The thread pool; .NET API reference, System.Threading.Tasks.Task.Run(Action), Remarks

claims.text: A program that hands its thread back on an idle wait gets through more pieces of work with the same number of threads than one that holds a thread through each wait, when many such waits are outstanding at once.
claims.source_hint: .NET asynchronous programming, Async in depth (a blocked thread serves nobody while an awaited wait occupies none); .NET fundamentals, ThreadPool

claims.text: Waiting for a file, a network reply or a database is idle time in the same sense as Task.Delay: the thread has nothing to compute while it waits.
claims.source_hint: .NET asynchronous programming, Async in depth: I/O-bound work does not occupy a thread while it is in flight

claims.text: A method must carry the async modifier for await to appear in its body, and an async method that produces no value returns a Task standing for the work in flight, which its caller can await.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference, async modifier and await operator; .NET asynchronous programming, Asynchronous programming with async and await: return types of async methods
